keyVerseText: Whoso privily slandereth his neighbour, him will I cut off: him that hath an high look and a proud heart will not I suffer.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew verb לָשַׁן (lâshan) originates from a primitive root meaning 'to lick,' but it is used denominatively from the noun לָשׁוֹן (lâshôwn), meaning 'tongue.' This connection highlights the physical instrument of speech, emphasizing the action of using the tongue. The literal sense of 'licking' metaphorically extends to the act of speaking, specifically in a negative sense involving slander or accusation. Thus, the root meaning enriches our understanding by linking the physical act of the tongue with the moral weight of harmful speech.
usageInScripture: The word לָשַׁן appears twice in Scripture and is consistently translated in contexts involving harmful speech, specifically as 'slandereth' and 'accuse.' This limited but focused usage reveals that the term carries a strong connotation of wrongful verbal behavior, whether by slandering or accusing others unjustly. The verb forms include Poel, Piel, and Hiphil stems, all emphasizing the active role of the tongue in damaging relationships through speech, underscoring the seriousness of verbal sin in biblical teaching.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding לָשַׁן as a verb rooted in the physical use of the tongue to slander or accuse deepens our grasp of the biblical condemnation of harmful speech. The tongue, as God's creation, is intended for truth and edification, but when misused, it becomes a tool for sin that fractures community and dishonors God. This word reminds believers of the power of words to either build up or destroy, calling for faithfulness in speech as an expression of holiness. Christ’s teaching on the tongue and speech aligns with this, urging believers to reflect His character by avoiding slander and accusation. Thus, לָשַׁן highlights the spiritual responsibility to guard our words as part of living a Christ-centered life.
keyVerseReflection: Psalm 101:5 declares, 'Whoso privily slandereth his neighbour, him will I cut off,' directly addressing the sin denoted by לָשַׁן. The use of this word here emphasizes the secret and damaging nature of slander, portraying it as a grave offense warranting divine judgment. The verse’s warning against the proud heart and high look complements the condemnation of slander, linking harmful speech with prideful attitudes. This verse calls believers to reject all forms of slander, reflecting God’s holiness by honoring others in speech.
